title: David Dhawan Is Retiring. His Last Film Stars His Son. Bollywood's King of Comedy Is Walking Away on His Own Terms.
excerpt: Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai releases June 5 and closes a 30-year career that defined how a generation of Indians — and their children abroad — learned to laugh at the movies.
body:
David Dhawan has spent 30 years making Indians laugh. On Thursday, when Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai opens in cinemas worldwide, he will stop.

The 74-year-old filmmaker, often called the King of Comedy, has officially announced that this will be his final directorial venture. He said it plainly during a recent promotional event: "I don't think I should do more. This might be my last film. After this, I'll just be Varun's father."

It is a statement that manages to be both deeply sentimental and perfectly timed. The film he chose for his curtain call is a collaboration with his son, Varun Dhawan — their fourth together after Main Tera Hero, Judwaa 2, and Coolie No. 1. It is also, by design, a return to the kind of cinema David Dhawan built his empire on: a clean, chaotic, family entertainer with romance, confusion, and a cast large enough to fill a wedding.

## The Plot: Classic Dhawan, Unfiltered

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai tells the story of Jass (Varun Dhawan) and Bani (Mrunal Thakur), a married couple whose five-year relationship collapses under the weight of clashing priorities — career ambitions on one side, the pressure to start a family on the other. After the split, Jass travels abroad and finds new romance with a character played by Pooja Hegde, setting up the kind of love triangle that Dhawan has been orchestrating since before most of his current audience was born.

The supporting cast is a Dhawan family reunion in itself: Maniesh Paul, Kubbra Sait, Jimmy Shergill, Chunky Panday, Mouni Roy, Rakesh Bedi, and Ali Asgar. The film runs a compact 2 hours and 16 minutes, carries a U/A certificate from the CBFC, and arrives in theatres on June 5 with a first-day 50 percent discount on ticket prices — a promotional move that underscores just how badly the makers want families in seats.

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

For NRIs, David Dhawan's filmography is not just a list of titles. It is a shared cultural vocabulary. If you grew up in an Indian household in the US, UK, or Canada in the late '90s and 2000s, you watched his films at family gatherings. Hera Pheri, Biwi No. 1, Judwaa, Dulhe Raja — these were the films that played on VHS tapes passed between relatives, on pirated DVDs at desi grocery stores, and eventually on satellite channels that became the soundtrack of immigrant weekends.

Dhawan's genius was never about subtlety. It was about precision — the precise timing of a physical gag, the precise structure of a misunderstanding that spirals for 40 minutes, the precise deployment of an actor like Govinda or Salman Khan in ways that maximised their comic instincts. He directed Govinda in 17 films. Even Govinda's son, he once noted, would not do that many.

## Health and the Decision to Step Away

The decision to retire is not purely sentimental. Dhawan has referenced health challenges in recent interviews, though he has not elaborated publicly on their nature. What he has shared is a sense of completeness — a belief that he has said what he needed to say, made the films he wanted to make, and that the right way to leave is on a high note, working with the person who matters most.

Karan Johar, who attended the film's teaser launch, called Dhawan "a genre-defining institution in Hindi cinema." Coming from a filmmaker who has himself redefined commercial Bollywood, the tribute carried weight.

## On Set, a Professional Distance

Despite the obvious emotion, David Dhawan has maintained that the set of Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai operated like any other. "When I'm behind the camera, he's not my son, he is an actor. I just need the result," he said. He praised Varun's growth over 13-plus films and described their working dynamic as built on trust rather than script — a mode of filmmaking that Dhawan perfected with actors like Salman Khan and Govinda, who worked on scene narrations rather than bound scripts.

It is a generational divide made visible: David Dhawan comes from an era where cinema was improvised, instinctive, and sometimes made up on the spot. Varun Dhawan belongs to a generation of actors who read scripts, attend workshops, and discuss character arcs. That both can meet in the middle, on the same set, in the same film, says something about both of them.

## What Comes Next

After June 5, David Dhawan plans to step out of the director's chair permanently. For Varun, the road continues — he has multiple projects lined up, including his role in the expanding Maddock cinematic universe. But the Dhawan comedy legacy, built one belly laugh at a time across three decades, will close its final chapter this week.

For the Indian diaspora, many of whom discovered Bollywood comedy through Dhawan's work, it is worth making one last trip to the cinema. The King of Comedy chose to leave on his own terms. The least his audience can do is show up.
author: Diaspora Desk
